Senses.Explanation: To keep the precepts is to remain answerable to their prohibitions. Poshan Haiming denies a simple reward-and-punishment calculation—keepers do not thereby rise to heaven and breakers do not thereby fall into hell—then asks what ‘true keeping’ is. Wanru Tongwei warns that rigorous keeping can become an obstacle when someone takes it as sufficient and no longer trusts that there is anything further to investigate. Changmu Guangdian's story of a rigorously observant monk shows the same tension: impeccable restraint does not itself settle the public test. Hanyue Fazang reports people who say they have labored bitterly at keeping precepts yet gained no ease, and uses their complaint to expose their refusal to investigate directly. Konggu Daocheng says he left home young, kept precepts with full sincerity, and exerted himself in Chan before pressing the point that the work cannot be borrowed from another. Guxue Zhenzhe finally asks who the keeper is. Across these cases, keeping remains concrete while its agent and sufficiency are questioned.

Senses.Explanation: The Fisherman who meets Qu Yuan is an identifiable classical dialogue figure. Wansong's commentary supplies the encounter background: the exiled Qu Yuan walks by the river and tells the Fisherman that the whole world is drunk while he alone is sober and that everyone is muddy while he alone is clear. Elsewhere Wansong quotes the Fisherman's clear-water and muddy-water song. A later Chan verse names Qu Yuan and the Fisherman together, declares both wrong, sends each home with his own song, and redirects the pair toward a road through the gate of birth and death. The corpus therefore does more than use a generic occupation here: it repeatedly recalls the same paired literary encounter and then appraises both participants from within Chan verse.

Senses.Explanation: Fisherman also occurs as the exact title of a work or poem, a different lexical object from the person it depicts. One prose passage names Fisherman among Qu Yuan's works and says he used it to give himself release. Independent Chan collections place the bare word in section headings above poems: one poem describes moonlight, reed flowers, a fishing boat, dangerous waves, and a cormorant; another describes years passed in a skiff and a fisherman's flute at dusk; a third describes a fishing boat, a thousand-foot line held within a square inch, and the search for a giant fish. Senses.Explanation: The phrase ‘Old monk’ is both an ordinary designation for an elderly monk and the conventional first-person self-reference used by named teachers such as Baizhang Huaihai, Linji Yixuan, Zhaozhou Congshen, and Yunju Daoqi. The human role remains the same across narration, address, and self-reference; those grammatical settings do not create separate senses. Its characteristic Chan use is humble first-person self-reference in monastic speech, conventionally translated ‘this old monk’ and grammatically serving as ‘I’ or ‘me.’ Baizhang Huaihai recalls receiving Mazu Daoyi’s shout; Linji Yixuan says he sits securely and distinguishes the visitors who come; Zhaozhou Congshen redirects a public interview by saying, ‘this old monk is hard of hearing; ask loudly’; and Yunju Daoqi addresses the assembly at his final meeting. The same noun phrase also refers in narration to an old monk: Wuzhuo meets one, a raised case begins with an old monk carried by two disciples, and a record introduces ‘an old monk named Puhui.’ Speaker self-reference, third-person reference, and definiteness are contextual readings of the same human-role noun, not different things.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 老僧罪過 says that 'this old monk is at fault.' In Chan dialogue it is a compact response whose force depends on the preceding turn. Master Yi uses it after receiving a pointed answer; Xinghua presents it as the capping reply that covers Linji's staged 'new arrival'; and Mazu returns Baizhang's own admission of fault. The phrase can accept, cap, or turn fault-language without naming a concrete offense, but these pragmatic uses all retain the same first-person self-reference and do not warrant separate senses.

Senses.Note: The phrase is neither automatically praise nor a guarantee that the action described is harmless. A commentary reports that people call Jinniu's carrying rice and dancing "pressing old-woman concern," then rejects their reading: it is "arsenic soaked in honey to entice people to put it in their mouths" (以蜜浸砒霜誘人下口). Elsewhere the location of Yaoshan's pressing concern is itself made the next interview question: "where is the place of his pressing old-woman concern?" (那裏是他老婆心切處). It can also enter verse, as in "pressing old-woman concern, laughing ha-ha, letting bystanders say long or short" (老婆心切呵呵笑，一任傍人說短長). Common frames include "only because" (the “only because” form, 24 occurrences; variant 祇為, 7) and "so very" (得恁麼老婆心切, 18). These uses support a forceful relational appraisal while preserving the possibility of criticism.

SearchAliases: an old woman's concern is pressing
Senses.Explanation: The phrase appraises urgently solicitous intervention: records sometimes praise it and sometimes compare it to poisoned honey. Literally, "an old woman's concern is pressing": old woman or granny (老婆) plus the concern being urgent or pressed hard (心切). The phrase is attested. It is a predicate applied to an unnamed interlocutor's insistent words or actions toward someone else, not the name of an inner state or a sentimental ideal. In the Linji–Huangbo–Dayu case, Dayu says Huangbo's old-woman concern was so pressing that "for you he exhausted himself completely" (為汝得徹困); when Linji returns, he says it was "only because the old-woman concern was pressing" (祇為老婆心切). In another exchange, a layman calls Huitang's concern pressing and Huitang replies, "I only want you to arrive home" (秖要公到家耳). The records thus show the idiom through predicates, agents, and replies rather than through a modern emotional gloss.

Senses.Note: The entry retains the literal gendered image because the corpus repeatedly connects the compound with an old woman's speech and with the broader collocation 'old-woman heart', which occurs 706 times in 214 texts; 'old-woman heart is urgent' (老婆心切) occurs 270 times in 129. The exact definition formulas yield two occurrences of 'one who speaks old-woman Chan' (說老婆禪者) and two of 'call it old-woman Chan' (喚作老婆禪), but no stable equation that narrows the label beyond the recorded comparisons and uses.

Senses.Explanation: Old-woman Chan is an appraisal label for talk or handling compared in the records with an old woman's solicitous speech. Masters apply it approvingly, critically, and ironically to sayings and encounters; it is not the name of a separate lineage. Dahui Zonggao asks whether the National Teacher's three calls may be called 'speaking old-woman Chan, dragging through mud and water' (說老婆禪，拕泥帶水, ‘speaking old-woman Chan, dragging through mud and water’), and elsewhere says that if he had initially explained everything this way, the student would later have cursed him. Huang Yuangong's letter contrasts Miyun Yuanwu's 'pungent handling' (手段辛辣) with people elsewhere who speak old-woman Chan. The label is also attached to actual old-woman encounters in the Floating Cup and Mount Wutai cases. Dahui Zonggao calls a line 'old-woman Chan in the great Tang country' (大唐國裏老婆禪), and Wansong Xingxiu asks whether someone with firm heels would consent to learn old-woman Chan. The term is therefore an attested appraisal label rather than the name of a separate lineage: records apply it approvingly, critically, and ironically to different sayings and encounters.

Senses.Note: This is the invoked pre-Chan figure, not the productive familiar epithet and not a claim that every longer compound containing the source term names Laozi.

Senses.Explanation: A rat entering an ox horn is a narrowing image whose endpoints are stated differently in different passages. Dahui says to press inquiry until there is no further place to investigate, “like a rat entering an ox horn,” when the stealing mind suddenly ends. In a winter-solstice exchange, an unnamed monk asks how a patch-robed monk turns around when the yin forces are exhausted and one yang returns; Xutang Zhiyu answers with the phrase. Another instruction says to press forward day after day and month after month like the rat in the horn, and explicitly says that then a living road appears. The image can also be used as criticism: one record says that a declining lineage becomes narrower and narrower like the rat in the horn, while Ciming scolds an answer consisting of the phrase. These attested contrasts prevent the dictionary from turning the image into a fixed declaration of either hopeless dead end or guaranteed success. Chan makes the narrowing horn a public answer, an instruction, a rebuked reply, and an appraisal of a lineage's contraction. The exact phrase is attested in the corpus.
